title: Ozempic and Mounjaro May Slow Cancer Spread by Up to 50 Per Cent. A Cleveland Clinic Study of Seven Tumour Types Just Changed the Conversation.
excerpt: The first large study to track cancer progression in GLP-1 users found significant reductions in lung, breast, colorectal, and liver cancer spread. South Asians, who face elevated diabetes and cancer risk, have particular reason to pay attention.
body:
The drugs best known for shrinking waistlines may also be fighting cancer — and the evidence just got substantially harder to ignore.

A study from the Cleveland Clinic's Taussig Cancer Institute, presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology's annual meeting this week, found that patients taking GLP-1 receptor agonists — the class of drugs that includes semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) — had dramatically lower rates of cancer progression compared to patients on other diabetes medications.

The numbers are striking. Among patients who started a GLP-1 drug after a cancer diagnosis, the rate of progression to stage 4 disease dropped by 50 per cent for non-small cell lung cancer, 43 per cent for breast cancer, 38 per cent for liver cancer, and 31 per cent for colorectal cancer. Three other cancer types — prostate, pancreatic, and kidney — also showed lower progression rates, though those differences did not reach statistical significance.

"Our study found that use of GLP-1 drugs, compared to DPP-4 inhibitors and other antidiabetic drugs, was associated with a meaningful reduction in cancer progression across four solid tumor types," said lead author Dr Mark David Orland of the Cleveland Clinic. "It provides early evidence that future studies are worth pursuing."

## What the Study Actually Measured

This was not a clinical trial. Researchers conducted a large retrospective analysis, comparing cancer patients who started a GLP-1 medication — semaglutide, tirzepatide, dulaglutide, liraglutide, lixisenatide, or pramlintide — after their diagnosis against patients who started a DPP-4 inhibitor, a different class of diabetes drug. Both groups had cancer and diabetes simultaneously.

The key metric was progression to stage 4, the point at which cancer has spread to distant organs and outcomes drop sharply. Across all seven tumour types studied, GLP-1 users consistently fared better.

Perhaps most intriguingly, the researchers also examined tumour tissue directly. Tumours with higher levels of GLP-1 receptors — proteins that respond to the same hormones these drugs mimic — were linked to about one-third lower mortality during the study period. This suggests the drugs may interact directly with cancer biology, not just indirectly through weight loss or metabolic improvement.

A separate study of more than 170,000 patients, also presented at ASCO, found a 7 per cent lower incidence of obesity-related cancers among GLP-1 users, reinforcing the pattern from a different angle.

## Why This Matters for South Asian Americans

The convergence of diabetes and cancer risk makes this research particularly relevant for the Indian diaspora.

South Asians develop type 2 diabetes at rates roughly four times higher than the general population, often at lower BMIs and younger ages. A 2023 study in The Lancet found that South Asians account for more than 20 per cent of the global diabetes burden despite being 15 per cent of the world population.

At the same time, cancer incidence among Indian Americans has been rising as diets westernise and screening rates remain low. Colorectal cancer — one of the four tumour types showing significant benefit from GLP-1s — has been increasing particularly sharply in younger South Asian adults.

The GLP-1 drugs are already widely prescribed in the Indian-American community for diabetes and obesity management. If future trials confirm these cancer-slowing effects, millions of South Asian Americans may already be receiving a dual benefit they were not prescribed for.

## The Caveats That Matter

This is not proof that Ozempic prevents cancer. The study was observational, meaning it tracked what happened to people who were already taking these drugs rather than randomly assigning them. Healthier patients may have been more likely to be prescribed GLP-1s in the first place, skewing the results.

The researchers also noted that for some cancer types, the sample sizes were too small to detect meaningful differences. Weight loss itself — a well-established cancer risk reducer — could explain some or all of the apparent benefit.

Dr Orland and his team have explicitly called for randomised clinical trials to test whether GLP-1 drugs can be used intentionally as cancer therapeutics. Those trials will take years.

## What to Do With This Information

If you are taking a GLP-1 drug for diabetes or weight management, this study is not a reason to change your treatment. It is a reason to continue it.

If you have been considering starting a GLP-1 medication and have both diabetes and an elevated cancer risk — as many South Asians do — this data adds another dimension to the conversation with your physician.

The drugs remain expensive, with list prices exceeding $1,000 per month in the United States, though insurance coverage has expanded significantly. India's pharmaceutical industry is developing biosimilar versions that could reduce costs dramatically within the next two to three years.

For now, the Cleveland Clinic data joins a growing body of evidence suggesting that GLP-1 drugs do considerably more than control blood sugar and reduce weight. The full scope of what they do is still being mapped. But the direction of the evidence is consistent, and for a community that sits at the intersection of diabetes and cancer risk, it deserves close attention.
